title: Return of Tensions in the South China Sea Was a Matter of Time
gist: Andrew Chubb (ASPI Center for China Analysis) argues that renewed China-Philippines clashes in the South China Sea since July 2026, including a violent July 20 baton-and-paddle fight near Second Thomas Shoal and a September 18 vessel collision near Sabina Shoal, were all but inevitable after a period of relative quiet.

insights.claim: After a period of relative quiet, tensions between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea are rising again, with clashes on the water sharper and more frequent since July 2026.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Renewed escalation in a key shipping lane raises regional geopolitical risk premia for Philippine assets and maritime trade routes.
insights.quote: Clashes on the water have become sharper and more frequent since July.
insights.locator: Tensions are once again on the rise

insights.claim: The return of regular China-Philippines clashes in the South China Sea was all but inevitable, implying the earlier lull was temporary rather than a durable de-escalation.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Investors should treat quiet periods in the South China Sea as pauses, not structural resolution, and avoid pricing out flare-up risk.
insights.quote: The return of such regular clashes was all but inevitable.
insights.locator: Tensions are once again on the rise

insights.claim: The most serious recent confrontation occurred on July 20, 2026, when Chinese Coast Guard personnel and Philippine marines fought with batons and paddles near Second Thomas Shoal, leaving a Filipino marine with a serious head injury.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Hand-to-hand violence causing serious injury marks an escalation threshold that could test US-Philippines alliance commitments.
insights.quote: Chinese Coast Guard personnel and Philippine marines fought with batons and paddles near Second Thomas Shoal
insights.locator: Tensions are once again on the rise

insights.claim: On September 18, 2026, Chinese and Philippine vessels collided near Sabina Shoal, the most recent incident in the renewed run of clashes.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Clashes are spreading beyond Second Thomas Shoal to other features, widening the geographic footprint of maritime friction.
insights.locator: Tensions are once again on the rise
